title: Why is the Dead Sea so salty?
description: The Dead Sea has water coming in but no river carrying it out. Discover how evaporation concentrates its salts, and where some of those salts end up.

sections.title: Water arrives, but has no river exit
sections.html:
The Dead Sea is so salty because it has no outlet: water evaporates, leaving dissolved minerals behind. Despite its name, it is a lake. The Jordan River brings water in, but no river carries the lake water away.

USGS describes this crucial difference. Water can leave as vapour; the salts do not make that escape with it.

sections.title: Fresh water brings hidden passengers
sections.html:
Fresh water is not empty water. It contains dissolved minerals picked up through contact with soils and rocks, as USGS explains.

In a lake without an outlet, incoming water brings minerals while evaporation removes water. That combination concentrates the salts. Think of a delivery service with no matching collection van.

sections.title: Some salt becomes solid
sections.html:
That does not mean every grain stays dissolved forever. NASA reported in 2019 that researchers had found salt coming out of the water as crystals and coating the lakebed.

The lake is therefore more than a bowl of concentrated brine: it is also a place where solid salt deposits form.

sections.title: The same process has a practical use
sections.html:
Evaporation also matters to local industry. USGS describes Dead Sea water being pumped into evaporation ponds, where minerals are extracted for fertiliser production.

The landscape's unusual chemistry starts with a simple geographical fact: no outlet. For the wider salt story, discover why the ocean is salty even though rivers taste fresh.
